According to Pace, one flawed assumption he held was that Iraqi citizens and military forces would embrace the concept of liberation. He had expected the Iraqi Army to remain unified and serve as a resource for helping build the new nation once given the chance. Instead, he explained, "they disintegrated in the face of the coalition's first several weeks of combat, so they weren't here."

Pace stated that foreknowledge of this collapse would have prompted him to push for additional troops from the war's onset. He further noted that had someone posed the question in January 2006 about expanding Army and Marine Corps numbers in Iraq, his answer would have been negative—at that point, the strategy centered on training and equipping Iraqi forces to eventually assume security responsibilities themselves.

That Iraqi force was indeed established, Pace noted, but the February bombing of the Golden Mosque—a site of profound significance to Shiite Muslims—unleashed dormant sectarian hostilities between Sunni and Shiite communities. This event further destabilized the country and derailed any timeline for scaling back American forces. In the aftermath, thousands have perished in retaliatory violence and bombing campaigns.

Despite these developments, Pace maintained, "Given what I knew at the time, I'm comfortable with the recommendations that I made," emphasizing that mistakes should serve as learning opportunities moving forward.

The general reaffirmed his backing of the original decision to invade Iraq, stating: "Twenty-six million Iraqis have the opportunity now. They are working their way through 3½ decades of being trod upon, held down, no opportunity at all for freedom of expression, for living their lives the way they wanted to, for picking [their] leaders."

Pace's tenure will conclude at the end of this month when his two-year term expires.

Separately on Friday, Defense Secretary Robert Gates made his first public remarks since President Bush's Thursday night announcement endorsing Gen. David Petraeus's proposed troop levels for Iraq. Gates emphasized that all of the president's top military advisers stood behind these recommendations.

Gates revealed that months earlier, he had tasked both Pace and Adm. William Fallon, commander of U.S. Central Command, with evaluating American options in Iraq independently—aware that Petraeus, the leading U.S. commander on the ground there, was conducting a parallel assessment. "I wanted the president this month to have the benefit of more than one senior military voice as he considered the next steps in Iraq," Gates explained, adding that he sought to prevent Petraeus from bearing sole responsibility for the strategic direction.

"While the analyses of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, CentCom and Gen. Petraeus varied in emphasis and approach, all of the president's senior military advisers are in full agreement with the recommendations made by Gen. Petraeus," Gates affirmed.

Gates argued that America's path forward in Iraq needed to preclude any perception of failure. # Pace Reflects on Iraq War Decisions

Outgoing Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Peter Pace has acknowledged that, with the benefit of hindsight, he might have made different strategic decisions in the lead-up to the 2003 invasion of Iraq. In candid remarks reflecting on his tenure, Pace offered a rare admission of miscalculation regarding one of the war's most consequential planning assumptions.

Pace conceded that his expectation—that Iraqi military forces would largely welcome coalition liberation and remain structurally intact to help stabilize the country afterward—did not match reality. Instead, the Iraqi Army rapidly disintegrated during the initial weeks of combat operations, leaving a security vacuum that would have profound and lasting consequences for the occupation and reconstruction efforts that followed.

Reflecting on this miscalculation, Pace stated that had he foreseen the collapse of Iraqi security forces, he would have advocated for deploying a significantly larger number of American troops at the outset of the invasion. This admission speaks to one of the most persistent criticisms of the war's early planning: that insufficient troop levels left coalition forces unable to secure the country and maintain order once major combat operations concluded.

Pace also addressed a separate, later decision point, explaining his opposition in January 2006 to increasing U.S. Army and Marine Corps force levels in Iraq. At that time, he said, the prevailing strategy centered on training and equipping Iraqi security forces to gradually assume responsibility for the country's security, thereby allowing for an eventual drawdown of American troops rather than an expansion of the U.S. military footprint.

However, this strategy was upended just a month later when the February 2006 bombing of the Golden Mosque in Samarra—one of Shia Islam's holiest sites—triggered a dramatic escalation in sectarian violence between Sunni and Shiite factions. The attack destabilized large parts of the country and effectively derailed existing plans to begin reducing U.S. troop levels, ultimately contributing to the circumstances that would later prompt the 2007 troop surge.

Despite these setbacks, Pace maintained that he stood by the decisions he made, emphasizing that they were based on the best information and strategic assessments available to him at the time.

What we saw instead was the wholesale disintegration of the army, which left a security vacuum that contributed to the instability that followed."

Reflecting on this miscalculation, Pace said that if he had it to do over again, he would have pushed harder for a larger initial troop presence at the outset of the war. He suggested that a more substantial force from the very beginning might have better filled the security gap created by the collapse of Iraqi institutions and could have helped prevent some of the disorder and insurgent activity that took hold in the war's early months.

Despite this admission, Pace was careful to defend the broader arc of decision-making that followed. He maintained that the choices made in subsequent months and years—including troop levels, strategy adjustments, and the eventual surge—were reasonable given the intelligence and circumstances known at each point in time. "Hindsight offers a clarity that simply wasn't available to us in real time," he said. "The decisions made along the way were the right decisions based on what we knew then."

Pace also stood by the fundamental rationale for the invasion itself, framing it in terms of the opportunity it gave the Iraqi people. Despite the immense difficulties, casualties, and instability that followed the initial invasion, he argued that removing Saddam Hussein's government offered Iraqis a chance at self-determination after decades of authoritarian rule and repression. # The Long Shadow of War: Washington's Reckoning with Iraq

WASHINGTON — In the corridors of American political power, few foreign policy decisions have cast as long a shadow as the invasion of Iraq. Decades after the initial military action, the conflict continues to shape debates about American intervention abroad, intelligence gathering, and the true costs of war.

CNN and other major news organizations have extensively covered how the Iraq War transformed not just the Middle East, but American politics itself. The conflict, launched in 2003 under claims of weapons of mass destruction that were never found, became a defining moment for a generation of policymakers, journalists, and voters.

From Washington's perspective, the lessons of Iraq remain hotly contested. Some argue the intervention destabilized an entire region, creating power vacuums that allowed extremist groups to flourish. Others maintain that removing a brutal dictator was justified regardless of the intelligence failures that preceded the invasion.

The human cost has been staggering. Beyond the American service members who lost their lives, Iraqi civilian casualties numbered in the hundreds of thousands. Cities were destroyed and rebuilt, only to face new waves of conflict as different factions vied for control in the aftermath of Saddam Hussein's fall.

CNN's extensive reporting from Baghdad, Fallujah, and other Iraqi cities documented both the initial military campaign and the years of insurgency that followed. Correspondents embedded with troops provided Americans with unprecedented access to the realities of modern warfare, while investigative journalists worked to uncover the intelligence failures that led to the conflict in the first place.

Today, Washington policymakers continue to grapple with questions raised by the Iraq War: When is military intervention justified? How should intelligence be verified before committing to war? And what obligations does a nation have to a country it has invaded, long after combat operations officially end?

As new generations of diplomats, military leaders, and journalists study this period, the Iraq War remains a critical case study in the complexities of American foreign policy—a reminder that military victories don't always translate to lasting peace, and that the true costs of conflict often extend far beyond the battlefield.

# Pentagon Officials Acknowledge Iraq Missteps While Defending New Strategy

**WASHINGTON** — In a Pentagon press briefing Thursday, Defense Secretary Robert Gates and Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Peter Pace offered a candid assessment of past miscalculations in Iraq while presenting a unified front behind President Bush's revised military strategy for the country.

Gen. Pace, addressing reporters in the Pentagon briefing room, acknowledged that military leaders had underestimated the complexity of the sectarian violence that has engulfed Iraq since the 2003 invasion.

"We didn't fully anticipate the depth of the sectarian divisions that would emerge," Pace said. "Hindsight offers clarity that foresight simply couldn't provide at the time. We've adjusted our understanding, and now we need to adjust our approach accordingly."

The chairman's comments come amid mounting criticism from lawmakers in both parties over the war's trajectory, with the death toll for American service members surpassing previous benchmarks and violence in Baghdad showing little sign of abating despite years of counterinsurgency efforts.

## Gates Stresses Unified Military Backing

Secretary Gates, in his remarks, sought to reassure both the press corps and Congress that the newly announced strategy — which includes a significant increase in troop levels — reflects genuine consensus among senior military commanders rather than a directive imposed from the White House.

"This is not a plan drawn up in isolation," Gates said. "General Petraeus, General Pace, and the entire Joint Chiefs were consulted extensively. The commanders in the field believe this approach gives us the best chance of stabilizing Baghdad and creating space for the Iraqi government to function."

Gates emphasized that the additional forces — reportedly numbering over 20,000 troops — would focus on securing Baghdad neighborhoods in coordination with Iraqi security forces, a departure from previous approaches that critics argued spread American forces too thin across the country.

## Addressing Skepticism

When pressed by reporters on whether the surge represented an admission that previous troop levels had been insufficient, both officials navigated the question carefully.

"Every strategy adapts to conditions on the ground," Pace responded. "What we're proposing now is informed by lessons learned — some of them hard lessons — over the past three years."

Gates added that while mistakes had been made, he believed the new strategy, coupled with benchmarks for Iraqi political reconciliation, represented the most viable path forward.

"I'm not going to pretend this war has gone as we hoped," Gates said. "But I am confident that the military leadership, top to bottom, believes this new approach is necessary and sound."

## Congressional Reaction Looms

The briefing comes just days before Gates and Pace are expected to testify before Congress, where they will likely face sharper questioning from lawmakers skeptical of the troop increase, including some within the president's own party.

Democratic leaders have signaled intentions to challenge the administration's funding requests for the expanded deployment, while some Republican senators have expressed reservations about the strategy's chances of success absent broader political progress in Baghdad.

For now, Pentagon officials are betting that a public display of unity — from the secretary's office through the uniformed leadership — will help build support for a strategy that carries significant political and human stakes.

"We owe it to the troops and to the American people to be honest about what's worked and what hasn't," Pace said, closing the briefing. "But we also owe it to them to move forward with a plan we believe in."

---

*This briefing reflects the tense political climate surrounding Iraq war policy in early 2007, as the Bush administration sought to build support for what would become known as "the surge" amid growing public and congressional skepticism about the war's direction.*

# Retiring Joint Chiefs Chairman Says U.S. Underestimated Troop Needs in Iraq

*WASHINGTON* — Gen. Peter Pace, in some of his most candid remarks since announcing his retirement as chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, acknowledged this week that the United States significantly underestimated the number of troops needed to secure Iraq following the 2003 invasion, a miscalculation he said contributed to years of instability and sectarian violence.

Speaking to reporters ahead of his departure, Pace said the initial force levels — built around a rapid combat victory and a relatively swift handoff to Iraqi authorities — failed to account for the scale of the insurgency and the collapse of civil order that followed the fall of Saddam Hussein's government.

"We didn't have enough troops on the ground to do the job that needed to be done, especially in the early going," Pace said. "That's a hard thing to say, but it's true, and history is going to record it that way regardless of what I say today."

Pace, who has served as the top uniformed officer advising the president, stopped short of assigning blame to any single individual or decision, instead describing the shortfall as the product of assumptions that proved overly optimistic about the postwar environment. He noted that subsequent adjustments, including the 2007 troop surge ordered by President Bush, were an attempt to correct for the earlier miscalculation.

"You learn as you go in a war like this," Pace said. "The surge was in many ways an acknowledgment that we needed more forces, more presence, more ability to hold territory once we cleared it. That should have been better understood from the outset."

His comments come as the Pentagon continues to grapple with the aftermath of the initial invasion strategy, which envisioned a leaner footprint than what many commanders on the ground ultimately requested.

## Gates Warns of Consequences of Jihadist "Victory"

The remarks were paired with a stark warning from Defense Secretary Robert Gates, who cautioned that a withdrawal perceived as a defeat in Iraq would hand extremist groups a propaganda and strategic triumph with consequences reaching far beyond the country's borders.

"If we allow ourselves to be forced out of Iraq under these circumstances, if we allow this effort to end in failure, the consequences for the security of the United States and for the wider region will be dire," Gates told reporters. "A jihadist victory of this magnitude, a defeat of this magnitude, would have ramifications for decades."

Gates argued that extremist networks would seize on any perceived American retreat as validation of their tactics, potentially emboldening recruitment and fundraising efforts worldwide while destabilizing neighboring governments already wary of extremist influence.

"This is not just about Iraq," Gates said. "This is about the credibility of the United States, the stability of an entire region, and the message it sends to those who wish us harm about what they can achieve through violence."

The defense secretary's comments echoed arguments made by the administration in defense of the ongoing troop presence, even as public support for the war continued to erode and lawmakers in both parties pressed for a clearer timetable for withdrawal.

Together, the remarks from Pace and Gates painted a picture of a military leadership reflecting on early strategic missteps while simultaneously urging patience and resolve to avoid what they described as a far costlier outcome should the U.S. mission collapse prematurely.

Pace's tenure as chairman is set to conclude later this year, with Adm. Mike Mullen nominated to succeed him. Pentagon officials said the transition would occur amid continued debate over troop levels, strategy, and the broader course of the war — a debate Pace's own remarks are likely to intensify.

# Outgoing Joint Chiefs Chairman Reflects on Flawed Early Assumptions in Iraq War

**Washington (CNN)** — In a candid assessment that offers a rare window into the Pentagon's internal thinking during the early years of the Iraq War, the outgoing Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff acknowledged this week that key assumptions underlying the initial U.S. military strategy proved fundamentally mistaken, particularly regarding the trajectory of sectarian violence following the 2006 bombing of the Al-Askari Mosque in Samarra.

Speaking in one of his final interviews before stepping down, the chairman said military planners had significantly underestimated the depth of Sunni-Shiite tensions that had been simmering beneath the surface of Iraqi society for generations.

"We all had the mindset that after decades of Saddam's rule, this deep-seated animosity would not come to the fore the way that it did," the chairman said. "I think that was a fundamental error."

The February 2006 bombing of the Golden Mosque, one of Shiite Islam's holiest sites, is widely regarded by military historians and analysts as the catalyst that transformed the Iraq conflict from an insurgency primarily targeting U.S. forces into a brutal cycle of sectarian reprisal killings between Sunni and Shiite militias. The attack, attributed to al Qaeda in Iraq, triggered a wave of retaliatory violence that pushed the country to the brink of full-scale civil war.

"That was the trigger point," the chairman said of the bombing. "Not just for the violence, but for a whole reassessment of how deep these divisions really ran, and how fragile the fabric of that society actually was."

Prior to the bombing, U.S. military and political leaders had largely operated under the assumption that a functioning, unified Iraqi state could be rebuilt relatively quickly once Saddam Hussein's regime was removed and a new government installed. That assumption, the chairman acknowledged, failed to account for the extent to which decades of authoritarian rule had suppressed — rather than resolved — communal tensions.

"We believed that if we built the institutions, the security forces, the government structures, that the society would kind of naturally coalesce around them," he said. "What we didn't fully appreciate was how much the underlying sectarian dynamics would resist that."

The chairman's comments come amid broader reflection within defense and foreign policy circles about the lessons of the Iraq War, as the U.S. military continues to grapple with the aftermath of a conflict that cost thousands of American lives and hundreds of billions of dollars, while reshaping the political landscape of the Middle East.

Military officials familiar with planning in the war's early years have said the sectarian violence following the mosque bombing forced a significant strategic shift, eventually contributing to the "surge" of U.S. troops in 2007 aimed at stabilizing Baghdad and other flashpoints.

The chairman, who is set to conclude his tenure in the coming weeks, said the experience underscored the importance of cultural and historical understanding in future military planning.

"You cannot go into a place like that and assume that removing a dictator resets everything to zero," he said. "The history doesn't disappear. It waits."

The Pentagon has not announced whether the chairman's remarks will be incorporated into any formal after-action review of the conflict, though officials say lessons from Iraq continue to inform current military doctrine on stability operations and post-conflict reconstruction.
